content: Volatility, in the context of chemistry, physics, and thermodynamics, refers to the measure of a substance's tendency to vaporize. It is specifically defined as the ease with which a substance transitions into a vapor state. At a given temperature, substances with higher vapor pressures will vaporize more readily compared to those with lower vapor pressures. While volatility is most commonly associated with liquids, it can also apply to certain solid materials, such as dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) and ammonium chloride. These substances can undergo sublimation, a process in which they transition directly from a solid state to a vapor state without passing through a liquid phase. The term volatility is frequently used to describe a liquid's propensity to evaporate. It quantifies the tendency of molecules or atoms to escape from a liquid or solid phase. The boiling point of a liquid at atmospheric pressure corresponds to the temperature at which its vapor pressure equals the surrounding atmospheric pressure. This temperature is often referred to as the normal boiling point. The volatility of a liquid is directly related to its vapor pressure. A liquid with a higher vapor pressure at a given temperature will exhibit greater volatility and a lower normal boiling point. For example, the vapor pressure chart illustrates the relationship between vapor pressures and temperatures for various liquids. Liquids with the highest vapor pressures have the lowest normal boiling points. As an example, propane has the highest vapor pressure among the liquids shown in the chart at any given temperature. Its normal boiling point is approximately -42.7°C, which is the temperature at which the vapor pressure curve of propane (represented by the purple line) intersects the horizontal pressure line of one atmosphere (1 atm) of absolute vapor pressure.
